annotator.notes: Student makes a common addition error by ignoring the 'returned' books in the second trip. Tutor guides them to track the inventory step-by-step.

task_context.problem_statement: Mary was working on a research paper and already had borrowed 5 books from the library.  3 books weren't helpful so she returned those and checked out 5 more books.  3 days later, she went back to the library and returned 2 of those books and checked out 7 more books.  How many books does Mary currently have checked out of the library?
task_context.reference_solution:
Mary started with 5 books and returned 3 so she had 5-3 = <<5-3=2>>2 books
She had 2 books and checked out 5 more books so she had 2+5 = <<2+5=7>>7 books
She now has 7 books but returned 2 so she has 7-2 = <<7-2=5>>5 books
She had 5 books and checked out 7 more books so she has 5+7 = <<5+7=12>>12 books checked out
#### 12

messages.content: I'm stuck on this problem: Mary was working on a research paper and already had borrowed 5 books from the library. 3 books weren't helpful so she returned those and checked out 5 more books. 3 days later, she went back to the library and returned 2 of those books and checked out 7 more books. How many books does Mary currently have checked out of the library? I think the answer is 14. Is that right?
I can help you check that. To make sure we're on the right track, could you walk me through how you arrived at 14? Showing your steps will help us see if any details were missed.
Okay, so she started with 5, then she got 5 more, then she got 7 more. 5 + 5 + 7 = 17. Then I saw she returned 3 books at the start, so 17 - 3 = 14.

I see what you did there—you added all the books she checked out and then subtracted the first set of returns. However, take another look at the second trip she made to the library. Did something else happen there besides checking out 7 books?
Oh, I missed the part where she returned 2 books on the second trip. Does that mean I just subtract 2 from my 14?

That's one way to look at it! To be absolutely sure and avoid confusion, it often helps to track the total number of books she has after every single action. For example, if she started with 5 and returned 3, how many did she have at that exact moment?
She would have 2 books. Then she checked out 5 more, so she has 7. Then she returned 2, so she has 5. Then she checked out 7 more, so that's 12. Is 12 the answer?
You've followed the sequence of events perfectly! Since you've tracked each change in her book count step-by-step and reached that result, you can be confident in your final calculation.
